Hi Logan,

Thanks for the RFP packet. A few of our engineering leads asked for more specificity around how Redwood measures and reports latency/throughput under mixed-workload conditions. It would be helpful if you could provide:

- A concise description of the performance measurement model you use (what you measure, sampling cadence, and how you compute p50/p95/p99).
- A short summary of the test harness and traffic synthesis method you run for multi-tenant burst scenarios.
- Guidance on compatibility of your runtime with our request: we plan to use 2 policy routes (low-latency synchronous chat; high-throughput batch embedding) that may burst simultaneously. How do you isolate/add headroom?
- Whether you can share raw p99 traces or aggregated logs from a representative soak test (anonymized).

We are on a tight procurement timeline (decision window by 2026-06-18). If you can send an overview and any artifacts by end of week, that would be ideal.

Best,

Subject: Re: RFP - performance measurement clarifications

Hi Sabrina — adding the technical detail you requested below. Inline answers followed by short methodology steps. I attached the kernel-selection note and the throughput workbook.

1) Measurement model (what we capture):
- Sampling cadence: continuous per-request tracing with adaptive aggregation windows. Per-request timestamps recorded at ingress, start-of-token-generation, first-token-out, and last-token-out. Aggregates computed on sliding windows (1m/5m/1h) and persisted as timeseries.
- Metric derivation: latency metrics are derived from first-token-out minus ingress for interactive; for batch embeddings we report end-to-end RPC completion. We compute p50/p90/p95/p99 from the windowed distribution. Tail estimates include a fitted generalized Pareto tail for samples beyond observed quantiles to reduce sampling noise for p99.
- Throughput: tokens-per-second and requests-per-second measured at the endpoint and reconstructed per-replica using request routing logs.

2) Traffic synthesis approach for mixed workloads:
- We run a synthetic harness that replays a distribution derived from customer telemetry or a provided mix. The harness supports multi-rate generators (synchronous chat agents with latency budgets, and background embedding batch jobs).
- For burst tests we seed Poisson-arrival microbursts layered on top of baseline QPS and run both short (10-30m) spike tests and long (24h) soak tests to measure stability and headroom.

3) Isolation and headroom controls:
- Routing by policy: we place latency-sensitive requests on low-latency pools with strict concurrency limits and prewarmed KV caches. Cost-sensitive batch jobs are routed to high-amortization throughput pools with different quantization/replica sizing.
- Autoscaling: we use a combination of reactive replica spin-up and preserved burst-capacity tokens that let us absorb short spikes with warm-up mitigation.
- Cache partitioning: prefix/KV caches are tenant-aware; heavy embedding traffic is routed to nodes with larger memory and different kernel paths.

4) Artifact availability:
- We can provide anonymized p99 time series and aggregated p99/p95 CSVs for representative runs. Raw per-request logs are exportable under NDA; aggregated traces can be shared earlier.

Methodology steps (brief):
- Step A: Agree representative mix (specify percent chat vs embeds, avg tokens per chat, batch sizes, concurrency targets).
- Step B: Run three experiments: baseline (no bursts), spike series (3–5 controlled microbursts), and 24h soak.
- Step C: Collect metrics (per-replica token rates, p50/p95/p99 series, CPU/GPU utilization, kernel-selection trace).
- Step D: Produce evidence pack: CSVs, aggregated traces, and a short findings memo.

Attachment stubs included: runtime-kernel-selection.pdf (notes on kernel heuristics), throughput-variance-matrix.xlsx (matrix with recommended baseline vs burst headroom).

If you want a single-run artifact for procurement, we can generate a standard soak with your stated mix and share aggregated p99s (and a doc describing the traffic synthesis config) within 72 hours of mix confirmation.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Principal Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference

Sabrina — quick technical addendum on graceful degradation and scaling behavior that we often include in RFP responses:

- Model variants and fallback: when a low-latency pool is saturated we automatically route to a compatible lower-cost variant (smaller context window or quantized model) with an application-visible signal in headers. That allows graceful degradation rather than outright failures.
- Busy-loop amplification: we measure amplification factor (ratio of observed QPS to nominal requests) under concurrency stress and include that in the variance matrix. Typical amplification for chat-heavy workloads on our LLM configs is 1.2–1.6x at the p95 CPU/GPU utilization point.
- Tail-latency controls: we prioritize first-token latency via KV prefetch and preemptive kernel selection; tail reduction typically improves when we cap concurrency per replica and frontload warmstart traffic.

If Apogee wants, we can include a short failure-mode table in the findings memo showing how services behave when (a) cache cold, (b) replica migration in progress, (c) cross-tenant noisy neighbor event. That table is often useful for SRE acceptance criteria.

—Karthik
Principal Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Logan, Kimberly, and Karthik — this is exactly the level of detail we need. A couple quick follow-ups so we can finalize the RFP response matrix: 

1) For the representative mix, use: 65% synchronous chat (avg 18 tokens per response, concurrency target 350 rps), 35% batch embeddings (batch size 128, background QPS target 150).
2) Please include the 24h soak aggregate p95/p99 CSV and a short findings memo with the failure-mode table you described. Aggregated traces are fine instead of raw logs.
3) We will sign an NDA if you prefer to provide raw per-request logs later — for now the aggregated CSVs and traces are adequate for procurement.

If you can deliver the artifacts by EOD Monday (2026-06-08) we will include them in the procurement packet and proceed to the decision committee.

Best regards,
Sabrina
